title: These Distilleries and Tasting Rooms Are the Future of Kentucky Bourbon
summary:
The spiritual home of bourbon has deep historic roots. Now, a new generation of distilleries is shaping its future.

The post These Distilleries and Tasting Rooms Are the Future of Kentucky Bourbon appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Kentucky is where whiskey fans go to immerse themselves in bourbon‘s legacy, in all its amber glory.

It’s also a living incubator for an industry that’s constantly evolving and innovating.

Even as bourbon sales have ebbed in recent years, tourism along the Kentucky Bourbon Trail continues to boom. Last year, 2.7 million visitors hit the trail, which meanders across the state from the Louisville city center to Lexington, rural Bardstown, and beyond.

There are more than 100 licensed distilleries in the state, supplying 95% of the world’s bourbon, according to the Kentucky Distillers’ Association. While many visitors prioritize the iconic producers, here’s a look at some of the forward-looking distilleries and tasting rooms setting the stage for what’s next.

A ‘Forest’ Grows at RD1 Distillery

Lexington

If it’s not aged in new American oak barrels, it’s not bourbon. But that criterion leaves a big white space for creative wood finishes—and that’s where RD1 is stepping in.

Shorthand for “Registered Distillery One,” RD1 was originally established as Ashland Distillery in 1865. The facility was the first to obtain a distillery license in Lexington. It shuttered during Prohibition, but in 2020, a group of investors, including former University of Kentucky football coach Mark Stoops, revived the operation.

Working with whiskey produced by Western Kentucky Distilling, RD1 uses wooden casks, staves, blocks, and more to add complexity and dimension to the distillate.

“We focus on the wood aspect of bourbon,” says Master Distiller Jarrad Gollihue. “We’re known for amburana wood, but we’ve also used sandalwood, eucalyptus, teak, mulberry wood, sassafras wood, apple wood, and balsam,” which is grown in South and Central America to shade coffee trees. They’re also known for experiments like bourbon finished with French oak staves steeped in maple syrup, creating flavors reminiscent of a stack of pancakes.

In 2025, RD1 opened a research and development distillery, including a tasting room, glass-enclosed lab, and 800-gallon pot still. The facility also includes an on-site “forest” for visitors to explore, which highlights the different woods used to finish whiskey, and includes a pair of selfie-friendly rope swings amid the woodsy backdrop.

Horse Soldier Farms: A Whiskey and War Story

Somerset

This year marks two important milestones in American history: the 250th birthday of the country and the 25th anniversary of 9/11. For Horse Soldier, which opened a $200 million facility in Somerset on July 4, the goal is to honor both.

Horse Soldier was founded in 2015 by a group of former Green Berets who had trained near the Kentucky-Tennessee border. In the days following 9/11, the special ops group became the first to enter Afghanistan, riding on horseback across the rough terrain; they became known as the Horse Soldiers. Their story became a book (published in 2022 by Mark Nutsch, a Special Forces captain and one of the company’s founders), a 2018 film (12 Strong), and now a bourbon brand.

“Bourbon brings people together,” Nutsch says. “It’s a distinctly American product.”

While their bourbon was originally made in Ohio, the plan was always to bring it back to Kentucky—and that’s where Horse Soldier Farms opened its sprawling 240-acre campus in July. In addition to the distillery and a barrel-aging warehouse, the space also includes an outdoor event venue and a wedding chapel. And as befits the name, horseback riding is also planned to become part of the attractions.

Next-Gen Tasting Rooms

Louisville

For many visitors, Louisville is the first stop, and they’ll find a lineup of new tasting rooms, including many that hail from out of state. That’s because, in 2022, state lawmakers signed a bill permitting distilleries to open satellite tasting rooms. That second location doesn’t need to have Kentucky roots, nor is it required to make bourbon. But these outposts can offer educational tours, tastings, and retail shops; some are licensed to sell cocktails, too.

They’re bringing a good time. Look for live music at The Last Refuge from Heaven’s Door, located within a former 160-year-old church. Meanwhile, Vermont distillery WhistlePig opened The Vault, a bar and tasting room in a historic bank building; don’t miss the opportunity to have a drink shaken via pneumatic tube, which whizzes like a roller coaster around the bar.

For those prioritizing Kentucky-made bourbon, visitors can try whiskey-and-candy pairings at Green River’s tasting room; fill their own bottles and watch live interviews for the Bourbon Pursuit podcast recorded on-site at Pursuit Spirits; or wield a long metal tube called a thief to pull bourbon samples directly from a barrel at Whiskey Thief. Taken all together, these tasting rooms show that bourbon is more than just a drink; it’s an experience.

Making Celeb Whiskeys at Bespoken

Lexington

Bespoken’s tasting room is housed in the bustling Greyline Station, a former bus terminal converted into a market. A glance at the shelves reveals recognizable names: Sable Bourbon, a marquee bottle launched with Taye Diggs, Morris Chestnut, Harold Perrineau, and Malcolm D. Lee, that aligned with the 25th anniversary of their 1999 film The Best Man. Private-label collabs with bands including Lynyrd Skynyrd and Whiskey Myers. “Kickoff bottles” and “victory bottles” for Ole Miss and other college sports teams.

Named for its focus on bespoke, special-edition whiskeys, Bespoken was founded in the San Francisco Bay Area in 2018, with the intent to use technology-driven techniques to age wine (and later, whiskey). While many purists frown on so-called “rapid aging,” the company secured star-studded financial backing from baseball player Derek Jeter and billionaire scientist T.J. Rodgers. Bespoken relocated to Lexington in 2024.

“We have no barrels here,” says John Gilger, a tour guide and brand ambassador for Bespoken. Already-matured bourbon is sourced from contract giants like MGP and Bardstown Bourbon Co. Then the liquor is manipulated via a battery of non-traditional gadgets like laser stoves to flash-char oak, sous-vide-like water baths, and shiny pressure cookers—all to whip up whiskey dreams in a matter of days.

Heaven Hill: A Post-Fire Rebuild

Bardstown

When a 1996 fire destroyed the original Old Heaven Hill Springs Distillery in Bardstown (including 90,000 barrels of whiskey), it was an enormous loss. After all, the venerable distillery makes a number of well-loved brands like Evan Williams, Elijah Craig, and Parker’s Heritage Collection.

Luckily, that wasn’t the end of the road. The company purchased the historic Bernheim Distillery in Louisville and relocated operations there in 1999. Following a $200 million buildout, the New Heaven Hill Springs Distillery opened in 2025, in time for the brand’s 90th anniversary.

The new facility will produce 150,000 barrels per year, with plans to triple that capacity. All this is set against a backdrop of environmentally friendly pollinator habitats, native Kentucky grasses, and nearly 600 oak trees planted across the property.

“Springs gives us a real distillery on the Bourbon Trail,” notes Master Distiller Conor O’Driscoll. “We haven’t had that.” And even though bourbon sales have softened in the post-pandemic years, he adds, people care about bourbon’s authenticity and want to learn more about how it’s made and meet the people who make it.

Looking back, “we’ve weathered all the horsemen of the apocalypse,” O’Driscoll jokes, referring to fires, floods, and Prohibition. The new distillery augurs well for what’s ahead: “It means that we are well set up for at least another 90 years.”

title: The Otherworldly Wine Caves of Italy’s Basilicata Region
summary:
The Sheshë wine caves in Basilicata represent a unique piece of Italian winemaking tradition unbeknownst to the rest of the world.

The post The Otherworldly Wine Caves of Italy’s Basilicata Region appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In 1964, Italian filmmaker and poet Pier Paolo Pasolini embarked on an ambitious project. He wanted to make a movie that told the story of the New Testament’s Gospel of Matthew, but through an Italian Neorealist cinema lens. All the actors would be untrained amateurs, the story would unfold with the confusion and awkwardness of real life, and it would be shot in locations across Southern Italy.

Puglia and Sicily provided the settings for the grand, dramatic scenes from the life of Christ in Jerusalem, but for his birth and childhood, when Jesus lived humbly with his parents, Pasolini needed somewhere that looked not just ancient, but mystical. For that, he scouted the region of Basilicata and found the town of Barile.

More than six decades since Pasolini was there, The Gospel According to St. Matthew is still the first thing winemaker Lorenzo Piccin tells me about Barile. “Pasolini shot [the film] here—that’s all you need to know to understand it,” he says. The director was drawn to Barile because of how compelling and otherworldly it is.

Located in the arch of Italy’s booted foot, Barile occupies two hilltops composed of the tuff from an extinct volcano. The town is a living testament to a unique piece of Italian winemaking history unknown to most of the world: the Arbëreshë wine caves.

While Italy likes to bill itself as a homogeneous country that has only recently experienced an influx of refugees, the peninsula has, in fact, seen moments like this many times before. The mountain towns stretching from Calabria through Basilicata and into Puglia have been inhabited by Albanian refugee communities since the 16th century. These people, known as the Arbëreshë, settled in Italy after fleeing from the encroaching Ottoman Turks in their homeland. And like so many populations who have arrived on this peninsula, from the Phoenicians to the Greeks to the Armenians, they brought with them their practices for making verë (wine).

The Arbëreshë dug out a vast network of caves, called sheshë in early modern Albanian, in order to make and store wine. More than 100 of these grottoes still dot the hillsides in Barile today. When Pasolini stumbled upon them, he determined they were the perfect setting for ancient Palestine.

The tuffaceous soil is easy to dig out, so excavating the caves and turning them into wineries and cellars was a surprisingly practical solution. “The caves maintain the perfect temperature and an ideal level of humidity all year, so there couldn’t have been a better place for storing wine, cured meats, and cheeses,” says Piccin, who runs Grifalco, an estate in Basilicata that makes elegant wines from the region’s native red grape, Aglianico del Vulture. These grottoes remained active sites of wine production and aging for centuries, with many of them even serving as homes for the winemaking families.

Over the past few decades, a struggling economy that has driven young people to seek work elsewhere, combined with the hygienic and logistical challenges of producing wine commercially in caves, has left most of the sheshë abandoned.

Today, only one winery, Basilisco, operates entirely within the grottoes. Winemaker Viviana Malafarina lives and breathes this place, confronting the challenges of limited space and maintaining cleanliness with admirable agility. She sources grapes from organic, sustainably maintained plots, like her Storico vineyard, where ungrafted, 80-year-old vines are trained in the traditional capanno method and grow alongside olive and fruit trees.

Malfarina is undeterred by the complications of making wine in the caves. “There is a treasure of enormous value here, both in terms of what has been and what might be,” she says. Her cru project, which offers four strikingly sophisticated Aglianico expressions, suggests there is much to be gained by giving the territory its due. The wines are sanguine and earthy, coiled with latent energy—a sort of vinous equivalent to Plato’s myth of the cave.

While other producers don’t do all their work in the caves, their wines still speak to singular Arbëreshë traditions. Elena Fucci, whose winery Azienda Agricola Elena Fucci brought international fame to the region’s Aglianico, employs Arbëreshë winemaking techniques with an eye toward sustaining the local farming community and maintaining these practices for posterity.

Using grapes from a pre-phylloxera vineyard, Fucci created a line of wines called Sceg, or “pomegranate” in Arbëreshë. Sceg is fresh and linear, but with a purity and concentration rooted in the past. “The sheshë represent the historical memory of this place, where wine has always been an integral part of the culture, from the very first people who arrived,” Fucci says. “It’s a point of reference that allows us to recount our story to new generations—the caves literally hold our history.”

Fucci ages her Aglianico riserva and superiore in one of the caves, where the bottles enjoy 360 square meters of perfect climatic conditions. Like the original excavations, this was a practical solution for her, as she actually needed more space in her growing winery. If an opportunity arises to restore and occupy another cave, she hopes to turn it into a tasting room where she can tell the story of these wines in the place best suited to it. As she puts it, “Why not tell the history of the place in the place that tells its history?”

title: Australia’s Most Isolated Wine Regions Are Leading a Quality Revolution
summary:
Western Australia’s three main wine regions—Margaret River, Great Southern, and Swan Valley—are producing soaringly good Cabernet, Chardonnay, and Riesling.

The post Australia’s Most Isolated Wine Regions Are Leading a Quality Revolution appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
“Kiss the hallowed ground,” my Western Australia-born husband tells me before I depart on a solo trip to his homeland. He’s mostly joking, but there is something sacred about the pristine, pre-historic beauty of W.A. (pronounced “dubbel-yew aye” by locals), with its incomprehensibly old soils and myriad native species found nowhere else in Australia—or on Earth, for that matter.

Western Australia’s isolation earned it the disparaging nickname “Wait Awhile,” in reference to the speed at which change happens there. The state’s only big city, Perth, is a 28-hour drive across the outback to the next big city, Adelaide. Despite its seclusion (or, in part, because of it), Western Australia’s three main wine regions—Margaret River, Great Southern, and Swan Valley—have earned an international reputation for soaringly good Cabernet and Chardonnay, ethereal Riesling, and violet-laced cool-climate Shiraz and unique fortified wines, respectively.

I didn’t plan on kissing anything but the rims of many wine glasses on my most recent jaunt around W.A., where I too once lived. But I couldn’t wait to be back on hallowed ground.

Swan Valley

Just 15 miles northeast of central Perth’s glittering skyscrapers lies Swan Valley, the second-oldest wine region in Australia and a treasure trove of century-old vines and historic fortified wines. The valley is significant to the Indigenous Whadjuk Noongar people, who believed the Swan River was carved by a giant rainbow serpent named Waugal. In 1829, the Swan Valley was colonized by the English, who removed both the Whadjuk Noongar people from their land and the nutrition-rich native yams on which they survived. Waves of immigrants—mostly Croatians—arrived in the following decades, shaping the region into the food and wine hub it is today.

“This river has changed dramatically since the European invasion,” says Dale Tilbrook, a Wardandi Bibbulmun woman whose traditional Aboriginal country is in Margaret River, but who has resided in Swan Valley since 1998. Tilbrook is an expert in “bush tucker” (native Australian foods), and she’s tasting me through a small selection of Australia’s 6,500 edible plants. We sip lemon myrtle tea, nibble on salt bush, and pop pink balls of finger-lime pulp in our mouths. It’s a sensory explosion of savory, earthy, citrusy flavors both unfamiliar and deeply comforting.

We’re on the porch of the original 1840 homestead of one of the colonists responsible for stealing the Whadjuk people’s land, John Septimus Roe. Today it belongs to one of Swan Valley’s largest wine estates, Mandoon. In addition to a fine-dining restaurant, brewery, and hotel, the winery collaborates with Tilbrook, who operates her bush tucker experiences from Roe’s homestead, which has been transformed into an Aboriginal-operated art gallery and gift shop called Maalinup Aboriginal Gallery.

Mandoon exemplifies the changing energy in Swan Valley. The hot, dry inland region known mainly for fortified wines—as well as Chenin Blanc, Verdelho, Grenache, and Shiraz—felt somewhat dusty during the 2010s, when I lived in W.A. Tourists still flocked, but the demographic skewed older and the region seemed to undersell its unique history.

Today, the tides are turning. A new generation of producers is reinvigorating the Swan, capitalizing on the newfound popularity of Chenin Blanc in particular. There’s Vino Volta, with its colorful range of minimal-intervention wines like pithy Chenin pét-nat and peppery, pizza-friendly Dolcetto. And there’s Corymbia, the brain-child of Robert and Genevieve Mann, fourth-generation members of a significant W.A. wine family, whose modern take on heritage vines across the state makes them one of Swan’s greatest assets.

Longstanding wineries are modernizing, too. One of the largest operators here, Sandalford, now serves a quarter of a million guests annually at its expansive tasting room and buzzy restaurant.

I derive comfort from the constancy of luscious Rare Muscat in the entirely unchanged 100-year-old subterranean cellar of John Kosovich Wines. The same goes for the molasses-like Pedro Ximénes Liqueur, made from 126-year-old vines at Talijancich. But even these ultratraditional producers are innovating. In 2024, third-generation members of both wineries created “The Swan Valley Old Vine Charter” to better protect and celebrate the region’s wealth of old-vine material. In a region constantly facing urban encroachment, the charter was well timed.

“So much has changed here over the last 20 years,” Arch Kosovich tells me. “What we’re doing here is cool again. It got forgotten about, but it’s getting airplay again.”

Margaret River

If Swan Valley is the forgotten classic movie, then Margaret River, 180 miles to its south, is the star-studded blockbuster that keeps delivering.

Jutting out into the convergence of the Indian and Southern Oceans, the region is a eucalyptus-dotted peninsula that’s been home to the Wadandi people for 50,000 years. While it produces just 2% of Australian wine, it nabs the lion’s share of national and international awards. Wines from “Margs,” as it’s locally known, include distinctive, waxy green bean Sauvignon Blanc–Sémillon blends and the odd Riesling, Pinot, and Shiraz. But it’s the region’s powerful-yet-slurpable Chardonnays and elegant-yet sturdy Cabernet Sauvignons that have turned heads.

One of the winemakers responsible for the region’s outsized success is Virginia Willcock, whose own trophy shelf groans, having spent 20 years at the helm of the region’s oldest winery, Vasse Felix.

“It’s the ‘feels like’ factor,” Willcock tells me as I sip Vasse’s latest top-tier Chardonnay, Heytesbury, its toasted cashew and salted citrus flavors lingering long after I’ve swallowed. “Margaret River has a Mediterranean climate with a maritime influence, and the ocean is very cooling. So when it’s 30°C (86°F), it feels like 25°C (77°F).”

The combination of warm, dry, sunny days and cooling ocean breezes, combined with ancient gravelly loam soils, towering eucalyptus trees, and unique vine clones creates wines that speak distinctly of their place. There’s gin gin, which Willcock describes as the “lowest-yielding, most expensive Chardonnay clone in the world to grow,” and there’s the heritage Houghton Cab clone. Both are on their own rootstock, since phylloxera hasn’t made it to W.A. The abundance of well-resourced, quality-driven wineries—and the lack of industrial enterprises—has kept the bar here extremely high. There are very few bad wines in Margaret River.

Compared to Swan Valley, wine production is relatively new here. Dairy and timber were Margs’s main industries until former doctors Tom Cullity (Vasse Felix) and Bill Pannell (Moss Wood) plonked Cabernet vines in the ground in the late ’60s. They were quickly followed by producers like Cape Mentelle, Cullen Wines, Leeuwin Estate, and Woodlands, who continue to benchmark the region.

But when I first arrived in Western Australia in early 2013, I struggled to find a Margs wine that spoke to 30-something me. Fresh from the buzzy natural wine scene in London, where I’d lived for over a decade, I craved more fun and gluggability from this classic wine region. I wasn’t alone.

“A whole new generation of winemakers came around all at the same time and were thinking the same thing: ‘Why isn’t there a wine that I relate to?’ Well, let’s do it ourselves,” says third-generation winemaker Nic Peterkin. He’s the CEO and general manager of his family’s longstanding winery, Pierro, but he’s better known for Chenin Blanc, “Albino Pinot” rosé, and a Portuguese red “Pirate Blend” under his own innovative label, L.A.S. Vino, which he started in 2013. Other producers like Si Vintners, Blind Corner, Dormilona, and South by South West popped up around the same time, each capturing creativity and vitality via alternative varieties and natural-leaning styles like pét-nat and orange wine.

Today, Margs has a wine for everyone. Some of the original “young gun” producers like Peterkin have added serious, single-site Chardonnays to their lineup (how could you not, given how gloriously good it is here?), while classic producers like Willcock are pushing the winemaking envelope with concrete eggs and wild yeast. It’s resulted in a dynamic and consistently outstanding wine landscape—a remarkable feat for one of the most isolated wine regions on earth.

Great Southern

Drive another 3.5 hours south from Margaret River, and you reach the only wine region in Australia more isolated than Margs: Great Southern. The five subregions that comprise Great Southern are so spread out that lumping them together seems somewhat preposterous. But for its hulking size (an area of 5,800 square miles, larger than all 700 islands of the Bahamas put together), Great Southern is sparsely populated by both people and wineries. Its landscape ranges from maritime to mountainous to continental. There are only around 50 wineries—40 of which offer tasting rooms—and visiting them requires a lot of driving. It’s worth it, though, for the adventure, unmarred natural beauty, and stellar cool-climate Rieslings, ethereal Pinots, and savory Shiraz.

I’m reminded of all of these things as I rumble across single-lane roads that pass for two-lane ones in my tiny rental car, dodging oncoming tractors and kangaroos, my phone reception long since gone. Between the towering 300-year-old karri trees, I catch glimpses of the dome-shaped Porongurups, one of Australia’s oldest mountain ranges. They impart a flinty purity to the Riesling in these parts, lovingly crafted by artisanal producers like Duke’s and Castle Rock. I also visit Plantagenet, the oldest commercial winery in the region (1968), and quirky producers like Express Winemakers, Brave New Wine, and La Violetta, who add color and youthfulness to the scene. The latter, especially, is one of Great Southern’s most innovative, with a range of bottlings that includes a textural, Mosel-style Riesling and a juicy Pinot Meunier. Classic producers like Singlefile are also experimenting with alternative varieties like lemony, herbal Arneis.

In Frankland River, Great Southern’s most inland subregion, I visit two leading wineries, Frankland Estate and Alkoomi. The ironstone soils and massive diurnal temperature swings here result in powerful, concentrated wines—including Bordeaux varietals—that retain beautiful freshness.

I sip salted lemon and ginger-laced single-block Rieslings at Forest Hill. It boasts the oldest commercial vineyard in the region, planted in 1965, a few years before vines kicked off in Margs. The second generation, Guy Lyons, with his senior winemaker, Liam Carmody, has taken this winery to new heights via thoughtful farming and precise, mineral-streaked wines.

“The Riesling from down here has a purity and rawness that reminds me of the Southern Ocean. I think you can taste sea spray on granite,” Carmody says. “We want to make Riesling that harnesses this power but is also delicious and expresses the vast, raw, pristine beauty of Great Southern.”

It’s more than beautiful, I think, as the black cockatoos chatter in karri trees above me and wallabies graze serenely in a nearby paddock. It’s hallowed. Suddenly, I can’t help myself. I kneel beneath an ancient eucalyptus tree, inhale its camphorous scent, and steal a quick kiss.

title: Can White Rioja Break Through?
summary:
The region's white wines have long been sidelined by its red superstars. But now is the time for white Rioja to take off.

The post Can White Rioja Break Through? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In 2025, the Rioja Designation of Origin turned 100 years old. It was time to celebrate, make new connections, catch up with industry friends, and collectively nerd out at a convention in Spain’s viticultural mecca.

Tuxedo? Check. Layers? Packed. Sturdy boots? Got ’em. Off to the airport.

On the docket were exhaustive tasting presentations, hundreds of wines to parse through, a gala to attend, and producers to visit. It would be an intense trip.

Fate has a sick sense of humor, though. Hustling into the first grand tasting in jeans, an undershirt, and a ratty old hoodie, soggy from the rain, was not on my professional ego’s bingo card. I was due for a lost-luggage fiasco, and after a few commiserating stories and sympathetic laughs with sharp-dressed colleagues, it was time to get over the humiliation and into the glasses.

The reds were magnificent, particularly the classics from old vintages. It’s Rioja, after all, the “Bordeaux of Iberia,” and age- worthy tintos have always been the star of the show.

But it wasn’t the reds inspiring me to think, “Damn, that’s awesome” in my inner monologue. Event after event, pour upon pour, it was the endless array of glorious white wines from Rioja leaving many of us rapturous with enthusiastic praise.

Rioja connoisseurs and professionals have long had a deep adoration for the classic white wines from a core cadre of old-school producers. But many aren’t prepared to grapple with the staggering breadth of greatness now coming from all directions and perspectives.

Rioja blanco has ascended from an if-you-know-you-know insider niche to a serious contender in a short stretch of time. But the road to this flashpoint has been long and winding, and whether or not it can be a marquee category for the region remains a question on many minds.

Always the Bridesmaid, Never the Bride

“White wines have always been part of Rioja’s history, but their importance has fluctuated over time,” says Mercedes García Rupérez, technical director and head winemaker at Bodegas Montecillo. “In the mid-20th century, white varieties represented just over 5% of the region’s vineyards and were often used to bring freshness to red wines, rather than to produce whites in their own right.

These white varieties remained a footnote in the region’s methodology and history—and the few that were bottled as standalone white wines were often of questionable quality. Sure, among the century-old producers of Rioja, Bodegas Montecillo included, there were indeed a few classic references of truly fine Reserva and Gran Reserva whites, but these were mere drops in the ocean of grand red wine.

Then came the 1970s. Along with positive press and political change—the end of the Franco dictatorship—came technical innovation from abroad. “New plantings and investments in quality led to better white wines, including barrel- and bottle-aged styles,” García Rupérez says.

Slowly but surely, the white wines of Rioja began growing from one-off unicorns styled by a handful of age-old producers toward a proper category in their own right.

Oversupply and declining demand stymied the ascendance of white Rioja in the subsequent decade, though, and reactionary regulation further impeded its growth. “In the 1990s, new plantings of white grape varieties were forbidden in Rioja,” explains Ana Martín Onzain, technical director and enologist for Bodega Castillo de Cuzcurrita. This induced an exodus of sorts, with winemakers looking outside the region for room to grow their white wine programs. “Important large wineries moved to areas like Rueda or Rías Baixas to produce white wines,” she says.

The turn of the millennium brought another policy pendulum swing, with white plantings once again permitted by the D.O. This time, however, it wasn’t just the classic local varieties like Viura, Garnacha Blanca, and Malvasía de Rioja. Near the end of the aughts, rare native rediscoveries such as Maturana Blanca and Tempranillo Blanco—a relatively recent natural mutation of the red—gained regulatory legitimacy, along with Verdejo from Rueda to the west.

In the 2010s, white Rioja gained momentum in Spanish and international markets, and its stylistic spectrum expanded dramatically. It wasn’t just about the rich Reservas and Gran Reservas anymore. Winemakers began embracing higher altitudes and fresher attitudes, with words like “minerality” and “liveliness” entering the Rioja lexicon.

However, the new regulations also sparked controversy. Allowing Verdejo seemed reasonable; the classic Rioja house Marqués de Riscal had pioneered its revival in Rueda. But along with the local grapes, expats Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc got the nod from officials, igniting a debate that continues today.

Tradition Meets Transition

After getting her foundation with fresh whites elsewhere, García Rupérez at Montecillo found renewed inspiration in Rioja’s barrel-aging traditions. “All the white wines I had worked with were young wines,” she says. “It was here that I began to understand the aging potential of white Rioja and how oak can enhance these wines, adding depth and complexity while preserving their freshness.”

In a similar fashion, Martín Onzain at Cuzcurrita approached the region after establishing a legendary reputation for crafting vibrant, crystalline wines outside Rioja. “My introduction to the world of wine in the 1990s was through white wines from Rías Baixas, Valdeorras, and Txakoli,” she says. Unlike García Rupérez, though, her take on white Rioja continues to lean toward more modern vibrance, not the golden unctuousness of the old school. “I’m not particularly fond of classic-style whites,” she admits.

But when it comes to which varieties should be permitted, she’s bluntly orthodox. “I think it was a mistake to approve those [international] varieties. They don’t contribute anything to the area’s identity or to the quality of the wines,” she says.

Francisco Honrubia disagrees with that sentiment, to a point. “This regulatory change encouraged innovation and diversification within Rioja, supporting the development of more modern and varied white wines,” argues the CEO of Familia Martinez Zabala, which includes the iconic producer Bodegas Faustino. “To some extent, they have helped modernize the category and broaden its appeal,” he says, while hedging a bit. “Nevertheless, as a historic designation of origin, Rioja should continue to focus on its native grape varieties.”

Like García Rupérez, he’s a classicist when it comes to style and views Rioja’s rich, oak-aged bottlings as a uniquely defining calling card for the region in a wildly competitive international market.

Over and over again during my visit, I sensed a back-and-forth between classic richness and modern freshness. International grapes versus native varieties. Round and round it went, with respect shown, but opinions echoing loud and clear.

Selling the Rainbow

Make no mistake, I’m a huge fanboy of white Rioja, both professionally and personally. But it can be frustrating to be asked, “What’s white Rioja like?” Do I keep it vaguely accurate and mercifully short by saying “it has something for everyone” or launch into a long TED Talk on its range of styles, subregions, and stylistic perspectives?

Either way, there’s no good answer, and that’s a problem when communicating with a global consumer who wants to hold on to something easily definable and relatable. That’s why New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc flies off shelves; Malbec is an entire country’s reliable trailblazer; and the superstar duo of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir is basically printing money in Burgundy. People know what they are.

“If white Rioja becomes too many things at once, it can become harder to explain,” says Gonzalo Lainez, the guy in charge of selling the stuff for Rioja Vega as the export manager for Grupo Príncipe de Viana. “The challenge is to make sure diversity doesn’t look like confusion.”

Billing oneself as being everything to everyone frequently goes unrewarded in the marketplace, and it remains to be seen whether that idea can cut through the noise in an overcrowded wine world.

Esperanza Elías, the talented winemaker at Rioja Vega, sees cracks in the wall and light shining through. “Rioja whites are experiencing a very well-deserved moment of international legitimization,” she insists. “We have exceptional conditions for producing great age-worthy whites, with their own identity and a very singular combination of ripeness, freshness, and depth.”

If she’s right and the trajectory can continue, white Rioja is on the cusp of a breakout moment in a global market clamoring for compelling white wines.

“Rioja already has a brand. The challenge is not to explain it from scratch, but to broaden the perception people have of it,” she says. “Is it harder to summarize? Yes. Is it less interesting because of that? I would say exactly the opposite.”

Bottles to Look For

Bodegas Faustino 2021 I Gran Reserva Blanco Viura-Chardonnay (Rioja)

Lemon cream pie meets baked green apple in this rich yet precise bottling, with enticing accents of Earl Grey tea, hazelnut, and toasted coconut. Finishing with a wet stone mineral streak, it’ll be superb at the dinner table.

Inquire with the winery

Castillo de Cuzcurrita 2022 Blanca Viura (Rioja)

Showing the structure of its high-elevation site with the intensity from old vines, this serves deep white orchard fruit and nuanced layers of spice. It’s impeccably balanced and will drink beautifully over the next several years.

Inquire with the winery

Bodegas Montecillo 2019 Viña Monty Reserva Viura (Rioja)

With toasted Marcona almond and Earl Grey notes hovering over an opulent core of peach reduction and lemon meringue pie flavors, this is a richly layered treat for the senses. It finishes with a squeeze of orange and citrus zest.

$66 Wine Chateau

Rioja Vega 2025 Maturana Blanca (Rioja)

This offers a head-turning take on a resurgent ancient variety, with excellent purity and freshness that counter its open, round texture. Green apple acidity cuts through peachy flavors, all topped by a dash of almond, hazelnut, and white flowers.

Inquire with the winery

Viña Salceda 2023 Entresierras Viura Tempranillo Blanco (Rioja)

This brilliant new project is sourced from two mountainbound sites and is bursting with personality and class. Ripe citrus and baked orchard fruits combine with polished oak tones, fresh lime zest, and a subtle minerality.

title: Put This Windy Oregon AVA on Your Radar for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay
summary:
Wines from the Willamette Valley's Eola-Amity Hills AVA get their liveliness from dramatic elevation changes and strong winds.

The post Put This Windy Oregon AVA on Your Radar for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Millions of years before Pinot Noir and Chardonnay dominated the slopes of Eola-Amity Hills, this Oregon wine region lay beneath the sea. Marine shales, siltstones, and sandstones developed a 5,000-foot-thick foundation of sedimentary rock. Then the lava came. During the Miocene Epoch, hundreds of individual lava flows flooded the area, creating blanket layers of basalt-based volcanic rock that would later weather into the iron-rich red clay loams that are prized by vignerons today

One of the 11 nested AVAs within the broader Willamette Valley region, Eola-Amity Hills has been an official AVA since 2006. Thanks to powerful winds moving through the Van Duzer Corridor, vineyards enjoy cool nights that bring acidity and liveliness to the wines. Volcanic soils like Jory and Nekia dominate the east side of the AVA, while the west side leans on marine sedimentary soils.

Walking through the vineyards, it’s not uncommon to find volcanic rocks and fossilized seashells within the same 10-acre plot.

The consistent wind and dramatic elevation changes—vineyards range from 200 to over 700 feet above sea level—helps wines stay crisp and refreshing. “There’s a brightness in the wines from this region that you really can’t find in many other places,” says Erin Nuccio, winemaker and owner at Evesham Wood & Haden Fig. The founder of Evesham Wood, Russ Rainey, planted the Le Puits Sec vineyard in 1986 and was one of the driving forces behind the creation of the AVA along with Ted Casteel of Bethel Heights Vineyard. “Russ saw the differences in the terroir of this region and felt the importance of labeling that and distinguishing it,” Nuccio says.

MOST WIDELY PLANTED GRAPES: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay
CLIMATE: A cool climate defined by the Van Duzer Corridor, where daily Pacific winds moderate temperatures, preserve natural acidity, and extend the growing season.
SOIL TYPES: Marine sedimentary and volcanic basalt

A north-south ridge creates distinct west- and east-facing slopes, giving wines from each side their own character. “The impact of the wind coming through the Van Duzer Corridor on a western-facing part of the Amity Hills versus the eastern side is so different,” says Maggie Harrison, winemaker at Antica Terra, who grows her Antikythera Pinot Noir in the northernmost part of the AVA. “The tannins that exist in the wines from the Antica Terra vineyard are from incredibly thick-skinned grapes because they’re facing the wind in that way,” she says, likening it to putting on a windbreaker.

In the cellars, winemakers from across the state come together to talk shop and collaborate. “We’re friends,” says Nuccio. “We’re not competitors; we’re colleagues.” Winemakers often share equipment, open up their tasting rooms to new producers, and work together on events.

The region’s collaborative energy and friendly vibes have been good for business. “Where as some American wineries have had a decrease in traffic, the wineries in the Eola-Amity Hills are seeing either slight increases or at least we’re staying steady,” says Kathy Lauer, president of the Eola-Amity Hills Winegrowers Association and co-owner of Bryn Mawr Vineyards. Wineries are opening dining rooms with esteemed chefs, dog-friendly patios, and even on-site cabins for travelers looking to road-trip through the region. A spirit of optimism and fresh energy runs through the region, giving wine lovers plenty of reasons to visit.

YEAR AVA ESTABLISHED: 2006
TOTAL ACREAGE: 39,200
PLANTED ACREAGE: 3,040
NUMBER OF WINERIES: 63 ELEVATION RANGE: 250 to 700 feet

Bottles to Look For

Bryn Mawr 2022 Zenith Vineyard Pinot Noir (Eola-Amity Hills)

The Zenith’s red cherry and baked goods aromas are like an amazing cherry pie spiced with cinnamon. The wine feels rich and luxurious on the palate, with a nice balance of lemony acidity and velvety tannins. The pastry theme continues as the flavor of a raspberry tart with caramelized filling dripping over the edge mingles with ginger and caffe latte notes. Spice, spice, baby. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Michael Alberty

$50 Bryn Mawr Vineyards

Evening Land 2024 Seven Springs Clair de Lune Chenin Blanc-Chardonnay (Eola-Amity Hills)

Claire de Lune is a 50-50 blend of Chenin Blanc and Chardonnay that was whole cluster pressed and fermented with native yeasts in barrel, with six months spent in neutral 228L barrels, and one month in tank. This new cuvée from Evening land opens up with aromas of apples, orange zest, ginger and cold, clean, mineral-laden well water. There’s a touch of spritz on the tongue, with equally ticklish flavors of lemon butter, wet stones and ripe Golden Delicious apples. The wine’s crisp and fresh mouthfeel goes hand-in-hand with its lively acidity. 92 Points — M.A.

$55 Evening Land Vineyards

Bethel Heights 2022 Casteel Pinot Noir (Eola-Amity Hills)

Blackberries dominate an aromatic set that includes loamy soil and the salinity of a maritime breeze. Cherry and lime-zest flavors match with a leathery texture, muscular tannins and juicy acidity. When you open this wine, make a toast to Terry Casteel, the winery’s co-founder. He died on November 30, 2023. Enjoy 2024–2035. Cellar Selection. 93 Points — M.A.

$80 Bethel Heights Vineyard

Bet You Didn’t Know

title: How One Man’s Obsession Revived Winemaking on a Tiny Italian Island
summary:
Compelled by his love for Giglio and his affinity for natural wine, Francesco Carfagna purchased his first plot in 1999. The rest is history.

The post How One Man’s Obsession Revived Winemaking on a Tiny Italian Island appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Most days end the same for winemaker Francesco Carfagna. As the sun dips behind Corsica, he sits outside his old windmill, sharing a carafe of wine with his wife, Gabriella.

The stray cats that live among their fig trees and fermenters nuzzle against his legs as he lingers in the afterglow. He gazes out beyond the rows of Ansonica vines that slope down the west coast of Giglio, an eight-square-mile island in the Tyrrhenian Sea. No matter what chaos the day may have brought—a truck needing repairs, a hired hand quitting, or, say, getting arrested for clearing the brambles between his vineyards—Carfagna seems to find peace reflecting in these last moments of daylight.

Carfagna, 78, has lived on Giglio since 1986. When he moved here, he was a teacher-turned-stonemason returning to a place that had “bewitched” him during a childhood visit. When he met Gabriella—a tourist staying at the guesthouse where he was building stone walls—he fell in love immediately. After she joined him on the island, he opened a restaurant, bought a windmill, and converted it into a home for his growing family.

Carfagna became a winemaker at 51. His son, Mattia, helped out in the vineyard, while his daughter, Irene, drew the bird logo that still graces the bottles. He restored abandoned terraces and launched his winery, Altura, devoting himself to the island’s Ansonaco wine and reviving a tradition that had nearly vanished.

For years, he did this work in relative obscurity, convinced of the nobility of his pursuit. Yet, in a life full of strange twists and quixotic undertakings, perhaps the greatest irony of all is that recognition has arrived only now, in the twilight of his career.

Carfagna has the look of a painter and the soul of a poet. When he mentions Ansonaco, his “golden wine,” he does so with a devotional reverence. And when he talks about the islanders who taught him to bush-train vines to weather Giglio’s extremes, he refers to them as “masters.”

Made mostly from the Ansonica grape, a.k.a. Inzolia, Ansonaco has been produced on Giglio since the time of the Etruscans. The wine has a honey-like hue and an aroma laced with wild herbs like artemisia and rosemary. For centuries, terraced vineyards covered nearly the entire island. The grapes were pressed in granite palmenti and then transferred to clay amphorae to mature.

In medieval times, Giglio’s wine was so widely loved that the island was featured in the 1596 book De naturali vinorum historia, perhaps the first Italian wine guide ever published. By the 20th century, however, Ansonaco—and Giglio itself—were in rapid decline.

After the island’s pyrite mine closed in 1962, the population shrank from about 2,300 to 1,200 today. Only a few hundred people stay on Giglio through the winter, Carfagna says. As families left, they abandoned their vineyards. By the turn of the 21st century, there were barely more than 20 planted acres left on the island.

“There used to be dozens of winemakers,” Carfagna says. By the 1990s, there were “just some old masters” making Ansonaco for their families and village festivals. There were no commercial wineries.

Compelled by his love for Giglio and his affinity for natural wine, Carfagna purchased his first plot in 1999. It was a maze of myrtles and mastic trees—“real beasts to uproot,” he says. “It took more than a year to clear the land.”

He thought commercializing Ansonaco might offer a lifeline to the neglected island. Instead, it left him “a little bit like the last samurai of Ansonaco,” as John Wurdeman, co-founder of Georgia’s Pheasant’s Tears winery and a longtime friend, puts it.

“We made wine for 10 years before anyone else joined us,” Carfagna says, walking me down to where his grapevines meet a sheer cliff that plummets more than 300 feet into the sea. “I’m the stupid, crazy man who decided to do this.”

While he has seen his Altura wines travel as far as New York, London, and Hong Kong, he has also experienced confounding lows. In 2017, for example, he spent 11 nights in jail for clearing thorns between his vineyards—technically protected land— without a permit.

On Giglio, the vines must be trained low, in the albarello style, to prevent them from being uprooted by the wind. There are no roads down to the vines, so they must be worked by hand. The island has gone years without rain, and rabbits terrorize the plants.

“Francesco’s vineyards are extremely tough to work,” Wurdeman says. “He’s not going for low-hanging fruit.”

Running a winery could be punishing off the island, too. Carfagna spent years distributing his own wine and showcasing it himself on the tasting circuit. But his hard work paid off when Altura earned recognition from the Slow Food organization. For decades, the group has awarded the winery its snail symbol, reserved for producers that practice environmentally sensitive farming and make authentic, terroir-driven wines. And last year, in perhaps the pinnacle of his career, Carfagna was named Vigneron of the Year by Gambero Rosso, the Italian publisher.

As Carfagna’s reputation grew, so did Giglio’s. Until 2010, Altura was the only commercial winery on the island. Today, there are nine, though only a few are run by people who live there year-round. Carfagna doesn’t hide his feelings about it: The winemakers he respects most are the ones who have made Giglio their permanent home— that includes his daughter.

“Everybody laughed at him when he started making wine, but if he didn’t do it, I don’t know if all these people here who are making wine now would exist,” Irene tells me.

Like her father, Irene has followed an unusual path to wine—and back to her home. She spent time in Russia, where her mother’s family is from. It wasn’t until she was working at a wine bar in Turin that she realized wine was her future, too. At 34, she has overseen Altura for a few years, honing her craft under the watchful eye of her father, who has traded fieldwork for morning swims in the sea.

She’s already made her mark, introducing a summer-friendly red made from Sangiovese and an amber blend called Emtivì (Malvasia, Trebbiano, and Vermentino). This summer, she teamed up with Milena Danei—a Giglio native who runs the Parasole winery—to host wine tastings with DJ sets by the beach.

For Irene, though, making wine has less to do with inheriting her father’s work and more to do with something larger than either of them. “I really believe in what my father started,” she says, describing everything from the connection with nature to the winery’s resistance against the pressures of modernity.

“There’s a richness here, which is not the richness of money,” she explains. “This is not only a job. It’s also a choice of life.”

Get to Know Vin De France: A Breath of Fresh Air

 

Behind every bottle of Vin De France- VDF is a winemaker ready to shake things up. These are the creative minds who take French grapes and, with a dash of Gallic flair and plenty of savoir-faire, turn them into wines that are fresh, fun, and full of personality—perfect for bringing something new to any gathering.

Vintners using VDF designation are part artist, part explorer: sourcing standout fruit from vineyards across France, then blending, experimenting, and refining until each wine tells its own story. From beloved classics like Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, and Malbec to under-the-radar treasures and even new, sustainability-driven grape varieties, these winemakers are constantly pushing boundaries and reimagining what French wine can be.

When you spot the Vin De France label, you’re really discovering the spirit of the people behind it: winemakers who honor tradition while embracing innovation. Their freedom fuels a vibrant, modern style that speaks to curious drinkers looking for something deliciously different, without overthinking the price tag.

Curious to learn more? Wine Enthusiast recently rated a lineup of Vin De France wines crafted from different grape varieties in various styles. Our standout selections are highlighted below.

Modern: French Wine, Reinvented

This is the trendy France: creative, accessible, and ever-evolving, where exploration blazes the trail and innovation is key. The forward-looking producers working under the Vin De France banner have a refreshingly modern approach to winemaking. Here, creativity meets diversity, resulting in highly versatile wines that always pair well, no matter the occasion.

Convivial Styles Across the Board 

Delicious to drink, and great to share, Vin De France wines are truly convivial—to try them is to love them. These bottles are easy to enjoy, made by a new generation of growers whose focus is on drinking pleasure. 

In tune with today’s lifestyle and modern wine lovers’ tastes, there’s a Vin De France wine for every palate and occasion. From casual get-togethers to formal events, for social sipping with light snacks or thoughtful pairings with more elaborate cuisine from across the globe, these wines foster memorable moments and joyful celebrations.

Freedom, Flexibility, and Flair

Vin De France brings a breath of fresh air to the French wine landscape. A contemporary take on the nation’s rich wine culture, the designation gives winemakers greater range, allowing them to source and blend grapes from across regions the length and breadth of France.
Winemakers working within this more liberated space relish greater flexibility, meaning more experimentation, and the chance to fully reveal their skills and personality. With their gaze firmly fixed on the future, they employ sustainable practices in everything they do, from vineyard to winery.

Diverse: Daringly Different

Ready to head off the beaten track? Vin De France opens the door to a new era of wines, from time-honored to downright daring. Producers work with a wide range of grape varieties to craft a multitude of colors and styles from classic to contemporary. So no matter your taste, there’s a Vin De France wine that’ll hit the spot.

From feisty orange wines made from white grapes fermented on their skins, to sparkling pét-nat (a naturally bubbly, bottle-fermented style that’s been produced since the 16th century), to fruity, chillable reds and edgy natural wines, these are just some of the bolder pours awaiting adventurous palates.

Vin De France: Bringing Wine into the Cocktail Space

Vin De France is ideal for parties on its own. But its playful, easy-going nature puts a contemporary spin on classic cocktails, too. Bright, juicy, and irresistibly easy to mix, cocktails made with Vin De France wines turn any moment into something worth celebrating.

Grab a VDF bottle and spice up aperitif hour. Kick off with a zesty white with citrus zing, a luscious red bursting with berry goodness, or perhaps a sun-kissed rosé. Mix up a bright, sun-filled Chardo Mule®, or a tonic-topped Sauvignon Special with cucumber syrup, a rose-scented Red & Roses cocktail with, or a sparkling Flower Rosé with hibiscus—for good (low-abv) vibes in a glass.

Light, refreshing, and just the right kind of indulgent, VDF Cocktails are where the fun really starts. Whether you’re clinking glasses with friends or treating yourself to a well-earned wind-down, this is a new way to sip.

title: Can Parties Like Rosé Disco Make Wine Fun Again?
summary:
Glitter cowboy hats, caviar bumps, rosé dance parties, and indie-sleaze DJs—are festivals making wine cool?

The post Can Parties Like Rosé Disco Make Wine Fun Again? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Ten bus stops away from our destination, the crowd camped out in the back began banging on seats, chanting: “Rosé! Rosé! Rosé!”

We were all headed to the Rosé Disco, a five-year-old wine-slash-day party that visits six cities in North America. In August 2026, over 5,000 pink-wearing rosé heads descended on a park in downtown Toronto to dance, sip, swirl, taste, and, for many, get a little wasted.

Across the park and competing for audiospace was On The Way, a ten-hour festival hosted by Community Wines, a Toronto-based music, events, and natural wine collective. There, indie sleaze, dance-punk, and electroclash DJs manned the sound system through the afternoon. Twenty- and thirty-somethings in Carhartts, crop tops, and sticker tattoos carried around bottles of hazy orange wines and biodynamic bubbles “like it was bottle service,” says co-founder Blake Pearson, laughing. 

Wine snobs can snark and judge either or both of these gatherings all they want. “What’s a wine event without spittoons, tasting notes, pins, and Zaltos?” they might ask. “Are events like these for serious wine drinkers?”

But the wine world is in the midst of a slump, spurred by slow sales and awkward generational shifts. Fairs and festivals like these serve as possible antidotes to downturns, with their community focus, appeal to young consumers, and approachable on-ramps to the world of wine.

At a time when standard tastings include three-figure costs and intimidating vernacular, these festivals feel fresh, engaging, and exciting. What can big wine learn from this? 

Build It, and They Will Come

Rosé Disco started over beer.

Gez McAlpine and his colleagues at Feaster, a Vancouver-based drinks events company that owns Rosé Disco, had just wrapped a beer festival. “It’s a lot of beards, indie rock, smoked meat,” he says. “But we’re getting 5,000 guys out here having a great time. What does that look like from a female audience?”

Rosé—ceaselessly approachable and internationally known—was the answer. 

Today’s Rosé Disco is a wine-fueled, all-day party. It’s headlined by DJ Felix Cartal, with other DJs spinning from 2 to 8 pm. Thirty or so winemakers, distillers, and ready-to-drink makers pour samples or full-sized glasses. 

“Rosé Disco does really well in areas with winemaking communities,” says McAlpine. “California, Arizona—places where you can showcase local products as well as the Whispering Angels.”

Is it a traditional tasting room, where brands can control their narrative and experience? No, it’s not. But it does offer producers access to people who are demonstrating an interest in wine. 

“You can have two-and-a-half-ounce pours of each and they’ll walk away,” says McAlpine. “Next time they go to a liquor store, they can gravitate towards a rosé they’ve had.” 

Nadia Senchuk, owner of Leaning Post winery (a small-scale, cool kid Niagara winery), poured at the Rosé Disco. Her newsletter sign-ups, available via QR code at her booth, went “gangbuster”’ over the festival. 

“We had lots of people signing up, though a chance to win a case of rosé helped,” she says.  Rosé sippers signed up and stuck around. “People have been interacting with the emails too.” A recent offer sent out to the 127 people who joined her mailing list had a 50% engagement rate.

Making Wine Cool Again

Across North America, there are other untraditional events doing heavy lifting to welcome in the next generation of wine drinkers. Los Angeles-based Good Boy Wine bills itself as an alt-wine festival, where ticket-holders can try sips from more than 70 minimal-intervention, organic, biodynamic, or naturally-inclined producers, including Scribe and Martha Stoumen. An array of DJs curated by independent record label Stratasonic provide the soundtrack.

Two years ago, eight wine industry vets created Dose, an all-sparkling alley party in McMinnville, Oregon. Their motive: to bring a community-driven festival like Printemps des Champagne to Oregon, a blooming bubbles region.

At the 2026 event, chefs, winemakers, sommeliers, and collectors popped magnums in an alley. Attendees passed around bottles of local sparkling wine, pouring for colleagues and new friends in souvenir glasses (and, as the night went on, into open mouths or onto twerking dancers). 

There were bubble guns and custom-made glitter bottle holders. Caviar bumps went around, as did snack platters of fried chicken. A DJ kept the pace as the crowd dropped it down, glasses held high. 

Dose brought in just over 300 attendees and sold 290 bottles in four hours—roughly 72 bottles an hour. “We sold out of pretty much everything,” says Kate Payne Brown, one of the festival’s leads and a winemaker at Argyle Winery.  

Party in the Front, Business in the Back

Wine-fueled dance parties aren’t new. Pearson and his co-founders drew inspiration for On The Way from beachside music festivals in Croatia, where everyone drank low-intervention wines and danced. There are similarly lively events in Beaujolais, the Loire, Champagne, Italy, and beyond

In contrast, wine culture on North American soil tends to be rather serious. Many people associate it with white tablecloths and polished glassware. Very few concert venues and sports arenas offer by-the-glass pours, and if they do they tend to be budget bottles marked-up at stadium pricing. 

How are new drinkers supposed to get into wine if the on-ramp is steep?

That’s why the Community Wines crew aimed to make it easy to turn attendees to wine drinkers. 

 “We’re not going super heady into the wine descriptions,” Pearson says. “Most people at a festival don’t care to hear the origin stories. That’s no disrespect to the winemaker—these guys love the wine, but what they really want to know is if it hits their mood for the day.

“It’s funny to see young Gen Z holding up wine and flexing with bottles,” he adds. “But that’s the way they will get introduced to wine, right?”

Beyond throwing a really good party, part of Dose’s motive was to get more people acclimatized to the Method Oregon category, a new series of sparkling wine-centric standards in the state.

“The Method Oregon category is having a moment in the U.S., but it’s been misunderstood—and we’re up against Prosécco and Champagne,” says Payne Brown. “I think events like this bring energy and connection, and highlight what producers are doing.”

Familiarization and label recognition were goals, but attendees also left with an emotional connection to Oregon sparkling.

The menu was by-the-bottle only, so guests would buy one to share.

“People would just go up to somebody and be like, “Oh my God, do you want to try this bottle?” Payne Brown says. “Everybody [was] interacting and sharing wine that they had purchased.

“We’re all in this moment of life, and it’s not just the wine industry—people are hungry for interactions that are pure delight and fun.” 

Filling Glasses (and Crowds)

Back in Toronto, the Rosé Disco was full of surprises. You might expect it to be filled with a monolithic demographic: young women who love the hell out of rosé. 

Yes, there were many women in platform sandals and Vegas levels of sequins. There was a high concentration of bachelorette parties. 

But there was also a 90-year-old woman in a cowboy hat and pink heart-shaped glasses. I spotted finance bros in their 20s, 30s, 40s, and up. “I heard through people it was a good event,” said one 40-year-old male attendee. “It’s a beautiful day. Events like this make the city come alive.”

I spotted groups of 60- and 70-year-olds camping out on tables and catching up, too. Friend groups of all ages set up picnic blankets, shared snacks, and took in the music. 

“It’s such a beautiful experience to be part of something fun, not stuffy,” says Senchuk. “It enabled me to target consumers who were unaware of me. It’s one of the only wine festivals I participate in, as I see the value of finding curious, new wine consumers.” Of the 500 people who came to her booth, 80 to 85% had never heard of the winery, she says.

The demographics of On The Way were similarly diverse. 

“We had a big percentage of Gen Zs, of the gay community, people in their 30s and 40s who were here for the music,” says Pearson. “We were super happy it talked to so many different people and resonated with people across all demographics.”

To Rosé Disco’s McAlpine, these events demonstrate the immense potential of wine businesses to reach broad audiences. 

“There are plenty of wine events that already cater to people that love wine, collect wine, and spend over $40 a bottle,” he says. Those consumers aren’t causing wine sales to decline, he argues. Instead, it’s those who don’t relate to mainstream wine culture who are opting for ready-to-drink options or hard seltzers. “And they’re the ones that are often ignored by wine events.”

title: This Summer-to-Fall Vegetable Dish Is Straight Out of the South of France
summary:
If you’re overwhelmed by the abundance of zucchinis and tomatoes this time of year, make Tian Provençal.

The post This Summer-to-Fall Vegetable Dish Is Straight Out of the South of France appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The end of summer is always a little bittersweet. But the cooler weather paired with the last burst of summer produce is a sweet spot worth celebrating. 

Cookbook author and master entertainer Chloe Crane-Leroux’s Tian Provençal makes the most of the season. Similar to ratatouille, but made with a slightly different technique, thinly sliced zucchini, eggplant, and tomatoes are paired with a robust sauce of roasted red peppers, tomatoes, and fresh herbs. It is then baked in the oven until the sauce is bubbly and the vegetables are lightly caramelized—making the most of bright, seasonal flavors without killing your AC bill at the height of peak summer heat.

It’s also downright beautiful, which is why Crane-Leroux loves serving it to guests. It feeds a crowd and seamlessly pairs with a wide variety of starters and sides, and she says, “it is really the perfect transition meal from summer to fall.”

How Chloé Crane-Leroux Sweeps Dinner Guests Away to Provence

If you can’t go all the way to France, hosting a Provençal-style soiree is the next best thing. Here’s how the cookbook author and photographer pulls it off.

Read More

Tian Provençal

Courtesy of Chloe Crane-Leroux

Ingredients

2 medium zucchinis, thinly sliced
2 medium eggplants, thinly sliced
3 large ripe tomatoes, thinly sliced
1 medium red onion, roughly chopped
2 garlic cloves, minced
1 red bell pepper
2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
1 (14 ounce) can diced tomatoes
1 teaspoon fresh thyme leaves
1 teaspoon fresh rosemary, finely chopped
½ teaspoon sea salt
½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
1 handful fresh basil, roughly torn

Directions

Preheat your grill to high. Place the red bell pepper directly on the grill grates. Char it, turning occasionally, until the skin is blackened and blistered, for 8 to 10 minutes.

Remove from the grill, place in a bowl, and cover with a lid or plastic wrap for 10 minutes to steam. Peel off the charred skin, remove the seeds, and roughly chop the flesh.

Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). Thinly slice the zucchini, eggplant, and tomatoes into uniform rounds, about ¼ inch thick. Set aside.

Heat the olive oil in a large oven-safe pan or skillet over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and roughly chopped red onion. Sauté for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onion is soft and fragrant.

Stir in the canned diced tomatoes, grilled bell pepper, fresh thyme, rosemary, salt, and pepper. Let the mixture simmer for 5 minutes, then spread it evenly across the bottom of the pan.

Arrange the zucchini, eggplant, and tomato slices following the form of your baking dish (mine is round) on top of the tomato-onion base, alternating them to create a colorful pattern. Slightly overlap the slices for a visually appealing presentation.

Drizzle the layered vegetables with a little extra olive oil.

Sprinkle lightly with salt and pepper.

Cover the pan loosely with foil and bake for 30 minutes.

Remove the foil and bake for an additional 20 to 30 minutes, or until the vegetables are tender and slightly caramelized.

Remove from the oven and let it cool. Sprinkle basil and serve.

title: How Chloé Crane-Leroux Sweeps Dinner Guests Away to Provence
summary:
If you can’t go all the way to France, hosting a Provençal-style soiree is the next best thing. Here’s how the cookbook author and photographer pulls it off.

The post How Chloé Crane-Leroux Sweeps Dinner Guests Away to Provence appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
On her first trip to Provence in 2023, visual artist and cookbook author Chloé Crane-Leroux felt like her heart was “cracked open.” During the trip, she was drawn to the region in a way she had never experienced before. “I was like ‘this is where I’m meant to be,’” she says. “I just felt like I belonged there.” 

Since then, Crane-Leroux has been splitting her time between Provence and New York with trips across the sea at least every two months, but her connection to France didn’t come out of nowhere. Throughout her childhood, she visited Paris and other areas of the countryside with her family nearly every year.

Her passion for cooking and entertaining also stems from her parents, who were avid hosts all throughout her childhood. “We just always wanted to have friends over, and that’s exactly what my parents did,” she says. “They had friends over all the time, and I just really, really loved that.” 

As she grew up and went off on her own, Crane-Leroux continued both of those childhood traditions. She regularly hosted friends for plant-based dinners at her New York City apartment and traveled to France. Next spring, she’s bringing fans along for the journey with her first immersive retreat in the heart of Provence at the Hôtel Crillon le Brave.

Over five days, Crane-Leroux will take attendees into her world with trips to local food and antique markets, an olive oil tasting, and hands-on cooking workshops. In anticipation of the retreat, we caught up with the plant-based host extraordinaire to get her inside tips on throwing an unforgettable Provençal-style party—sans meat. Whether you want to celebrate seasonal produce, save money while serving farmers’ market fare, or just level up your hosting game, read on for Crane-Leroux’s tips on being the consummate host.

Open Up with Apéro

“Hosting doesn’t have to be scary,” Crane-Leroux says. “A lot of people get intimidated because they want it to be perfect and they overthink it.” That’s why she insists that the path to becoming a better host starts with small steps.

“My favorite thing is apéro, which is basically a French happy hour,” she says. All you need are some small bites and drinks, which Crane-Leroux says can last the whole evening or can trickle into a full dinner. “It’s the perfect way to start hosting because it’s not a full meal and it doesn’t feel so extravagant.”

Wine is Crane-Leroux’s beverage pairing of choice, especially when looking for ease. “In the summer, I love a glass of crisp rosé, especially if we’re starting with little bites,” she says. Sometimes, in the fall or winter, she’ll gravitate towards a red wine—”they’re a bit cozier”—but she enjoys whites year round. “You can never go wrong with a Sancerre or a Chablis.”

While she rarely enjoys cocktails, Crane-Leroux will sometimes indulge in a wine spritz. If you’re up to the challenge of making it at home, go for her favorite combo: a Lillet spritz with a wedge of grapefruit.

Showcase Fresh, Seasonal Ingredients

Whether you’re focusing on snacks or a sit-down dinner, Crane-Leroux is all about celebrating the seasons—even when it comes to tablescapes and decor. She incorporates seasonal vegetables into the floral arrangements or goes full-on produce-focused, like this whimsical tomato tablescape. The rest of the table setting builds on this rustic approach with mismatched wine glasses and candlesticks of varying heights. Crane-Leroux says that this “adds this kind of coziness that everybody loves at a dinner.”

Crane-Leroux also considers seasonality and visual presentation while planning her menus.

“Going to the farmers’ market and getting inspired by what is out there is the best way to come up with a recipe,” she says. “Honing into these key ingredients and eating in a way that just feels like how the earth intended is so great.”

Obviously, this changes throughout the year. In summer and early fall when the tomatoes and zucchini are still really good, Crane-Leroux likes to serve Tian Provençal. Similar to ratatouille but with a prettier presentation, the traditional dish spotlights fresh produce and looks absolutely gorgeous on the dinner table.

If you’re overwhelmed by the abundance of zucchinis and tomatoes this time of year, make Tian Provençal.

Read More

Galettes and rustic tarts are another eye-catching way that Crane-Leroux likes to center seasonal produce. They’re endlessly adaptable and deceptively easy, especially considering how impressive they appear.

“Truly, you can put anything on puff pastry, and I think it would be amazing,” she says. In the summertime and early fall, this often manifests as tomato or zucchini galettes, while cooler months lend themselves well to winter squashes.

Wine Picks Should Elevate the Produce

Plant-based food often gets a bad rap for being difficult to pair, but Crane-Leroux insists that couldn’t be farther from the truth.

“Wine comes from the earth and plant-based food comes from the earth,” she says. “The flavors of the wine can be complementary to a specific vegetable,” she says. “So you can really take dishes that have those particular ingredients and tie it back to a certain wine.”

Have you ever tasted a wine that distinctly feels like biting into a tomato? Crane-Leroux has, and she finds that pairing those kinds of wines with a dish featuring farm-fresh heirloom tomatoes beautifully elevates the flavors of each. She also loves pairing an earthy Lambrusco with red sauce pizza or a rich Port with cherry pie.

“A wine that brings those flavors out will also just make the dish even better,” Crane-Leroux says.

Let Guests Handle Dessert—But Add a Signature Touch

When guests inevitably offer to bring something, Crane-Leroux will often concede dessert. 

“It lifts a little bit of weight off of me from cooking,” she says, and it can add a fun element of surprise to the evening if you’re not quite sure what they’re bringing. Even so, she likes to prepare some sort of accompaniment for dessert to add a homemade feeling and an extra special touch. This could take the shape of anything from ice cream or caramel sauce to shaved chocolate or edible flowers to decorate. 

“You didn’t do a full-blown dessert—your guest brought that,” she says, “but then adding that little touch as the host, even just to make the dish prettier, I think that is the best of both worlds.”
